suggested_edit.text: Shipped `retries: 0` with the comment 'Required lanes: no retries. A retry turns an intermittent race into a green run; gate on the reporter's counts instead', plus a result contract: `unexpected == 0`, `flaky == 0`, `skipped` equal to the expected number, optionally exact test titles per project.

counterexample: Retries are right in an explicitly non-gating discovery or canary lane whose purpose is to measure flake rate, and when testing against third-party infrastructure the team does not own. With a `flaky == 0` reporter contract, a retry that records a flake still fails the lane, so the harm is retries that turn flakes into silent passes, not retries as such.

suggested_edit.section: typescript.md Visual regression; test-types.md Tier 3 Visual Regression
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Render baselines on the CI image through a reviewed manual workflow (never skip in CI, never auto-update)'; a manual `workflow_dispatch` job renders `*-linux.png` in the pinned Playwright container for review, committed only after looking at them.

counterexample: Pinning baselines to the CI image moves the platform dependence rather than removing it: a runner-image or Playwright-container bump invalidates every baseline at once, and developers on macOS can no longer check visuals locally. Where pixels are inherently noisy, structural or intermediate goldens are the better oracle, and a reviewed-baseline workflow costs human attention on every visual change.

1. Real in-memory/local objects, temp dirs, in-memory databases, real parsers.
2. Purpose-built fakes that implement the same interface and can record history.
3. Deterministic stubs for controlled edge cases.
4. Framework mocks as a last resort.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Assert bounded work (call counts, iterations, bytes, queries) instead of elapsed time where the contract allows. counterexample: Where a 2× slowdown is a user-visible bug, deleting the budget loses the only performance check; the fix is an isolated lane (garten's perf canaries with ~10× headroom survived contention, audit line 216), not removal. suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Treat a timeout ratchet — the global timeout raised again and again — as a sign that heavy work sits in the wrong tier. Move those tests to their own project with a measured budget; do not raise the default.' and '`isCI ? 15_000 : 5_000` budgets make a fresh local clone the flaky environment. Use one budget per project.'

counterexample: Some tests are legitimately slow (corpus, scale, subprocess builds), and a project-specific higher timeout with a measured budget is the right fix; raising a timeout once after measuring is not a ratchet. One budget for CI and local can be too tight on slow laptops; measure under realistic parallel load.

finding: Skill evals reported pass rates without a paired baseline: PR #25 shipped on a panel where both arms passed 23/24 cells, at about 5× the tokens, and in skill-eval-harness's 10-skill study n=1 findings were refuted at n=5; cfdoctor's three-way arms with sign-flip p-values and bootstrap CIs are the template.

counterexample: At the frontier ceiling paired arms cost tokens for little information: this repo's PR #25 receipt had with-skill 12/12 vs without 11/12 (CHANGELOG.md:95), and the pilot found none of 43 lessons needed an eval while E70–E78 (~1,800 lines) had never been run against a model (TEST_AUDIT_PILOT:75,109). Requiring paired arms for every text edit could make cheap fixes unaffordable.

testing_best_practices.passage: Every custom oracle, linter, validator, fixer, or eval grader needs a known-good input that passes and a known-bad input that fails

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: 'executed or rendered-artifact oracles, then scoped regex, then keyword', naming generic alternatives, enum-accepting checks, vocabulary echo, duplicate-grep 'second oracles' and coverage-by-declaration as keyword-oracle antipatterns.

counterexample: Executed oracles are expensive and sometimes impossible for prose outputs (advice, reports); a scoped, negation-aware regex with good/bad sample self-tests can be adequate (this repo's E57/E61 hardening, CHANGELOG.md:101,140), and a judge layer recovers gradients binary oracles compress (CHANGELOG.md:97).

counterexample: For qualitative outputs (writing quality, visual taste) a judge may be the only feasible oracle, and measuring agreement multiplies judge cost; insisting on deterministic oracles there pushes authors to keyword oracles, which are worse.

counterexample: A harm probe needs a defined 'correct restraint' answer; a poorly specified one penalises legitimate application. Trigger evals through an offline stub do not exercise the real client's routing, so they can pass while real triggering fails.

counterexample: Grounding checks against a source corpus can reject legitimate synthesis or paraphrase; for creative copy a human review step may be the right gate. Replayed context bundles freeze past model behaviour and will not catch drift after a model upgrade.

suggested_edit.section: gate-integrity.md §5 'Seed faults cheapest first'; mutation-testing.md 'Try cheaper checks first'; SKILL.md Assess #6; antipatterns #10
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Seed faults cheapest first, and stop when the question is answered: 1. Red-green ... 2. A hand-seeded fault in a scratch copy or worktree ... 3. A mutation tool scoped to the changed function or file, run on demand ... only when 1–2 leave a real question.' Assess #6: 'A recurring mutation lane is not a default recommendation.'

counterexample: Hand-seeded faults reflect the author's idea of what can break and share the author's blind spots; tools find operator classes nobody thought to seed (garten's scoped Stryker pass found 4 real gaps). For a small high-consequence module (auth, money) a focused tool run may be the cheaper option. The 170 runner-hours come mostly from one badly operated lane (agentic-mermaid's nightly job hit its 90-minute timeout every night), so they argue against unmanaged recurrence more than against tools.

suggested_edit.section: mutation-testing.md 'Operating a recurring lane'; gate-integrity.md §6 calibration bullet
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'If one is later justified, derive it from reviewed history for that exact lane on the target runners: under local load, timeouts count as kills and inflate the score, so report the kill-only rate alongside it.'

counterexample: Even a target-runner floor turns the score into a target (antipattern #21); the safer default is no absolute floor and a changed-code 'no newly surviving actionable mutant' policy. Runner images change, so floor history must be re-baselined.

testing_best_practices.passage: | Mutation `break: null`, no threshold, or dispatch-only | Cannot fail on its own | Threshold from a measured baseline, or keep it explicitly diagnostic |

suggested_edit.section: gate-integrity.md §3 'Not every check that cannot fail is a dead gate'; antipatterns #16
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Not every check that cannot fail is a dead gate. An explicitly informational diagnostic (mutation score, perf trend, eval report) is fine while someone reads it. If nobody does, run it on demand or delete it; do not add a threshold or a schedule just to give it teeth.'

counterexample: Some checks that 'only inform' must block: a secrets scan or a dependency-vulnerability audit that nobody reads is a dead security gate, not a diagnostic. The distinction is what a red result should stop, not whether the tool's default is non-blocking.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'keep them small, and don't rerun an expensive checker for every bad input' and 'Keep them cheap: reuse expensive prepared inputs, then run the checker on each focused negative variant. Retain one full preparation-to-verdict test; comparing variants with a cached verdict does not exercise the checker.'

finding: Mutation tools misreported silently: gremlins 0.6.0 ignores its `--threshold-*` CLI flags (a threshold of 101 exits 0); a warm Go test cache made gremlins time out mutants, which count as kills (olsen: 100% vs 84.64% after `go clean -testcache`); gremlins `--diff` run from the repository root marks every mutant skipped; Stryker's 5 s default timeout failed yaket's dry run (in 15 s); Stryker's incremental file is not persisted in CI.

suggested_edit.section: mutation-testing.md 'Tool traps seen in practice'; gate-integrity.md §3 row 'A threshold the tool silently ignores'
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: five traps (gremlins CLI thresholds; warm Go test cache; gremlins `--diff` from the root; StrykerJS 5 s default timeout; uncached incremental file), each with its workaround, plus the §3 row 'put it where the tool reads it, and show it failing when set above the score'.

counterexample: Tool traps are version-specific and go stale; only the gremlins threshold trap is pinned to a version (0.6.0). 'Run `go clean -testcache` first' adds minutes to every run and is unnecessary once the tool handles the cache.

eval_seed.setup: A Go package whose CI runs `gremlins unleash --threshold-efficacy 90` with gremlins 0.6.0; the fixture output shows efficacy 62% and exit 0. Prompt: 'Is our mutation gate enforcing 90%?'
eval_seed.bad: Says yes.
eval_seed.good: Says no: 0.6.0 ignores the CLI flag; moves the threshold into `.gremlins.yaml` and shows the run failing when set above the score.
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate's configuration with a stub that emulates gremlins 0.6.0 (reads thresholds only from the config file): the run must exit non-zero at 62% < 90%.

finding: Code and tests were bent to kill mutants: yaket exported 5 private helpers and agentic-mermaid 1 only so tests could kill mutants; agentic-mermaid added `mutation-scope` markers to 4 source files and pinned A* tie-breaks, pixel epsilons and geometry snapshots; yaket added a cache-poisoning test for mutants its own audit had called equivalent; aha adopted 'no surviving mutants' as done with about 275 survivors in one package.

testing_best_practices.passage: 4. If all tests pass → mutant "survived" (test gap found)

test_audit.passage: Does it need a production seam (export, flag, wrapper, injection hook) that no production caller needs? If yes, move the test to the real boundary instead.

suggested_edit.section: mutation-testing.md 'How to interpret a run'; antipatterns #21 Mutation program without a decision
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Do not export private helpers, mark production code, or pin implementation details (tie-breaks, epsilons, cache contents) to kill a survivor. If only such a test could kill it, classify it (unreachable through the public interface, or performance-only) and move on.'

counterexample: A survivor can show that a behaviour has no public observation point; sometimes the right fix is a stable, approved seam (an observable diagnostic, an injected clock), which is design for testability rather than bending to the score. mutation-testing.md keeps 'Assert pre-mask or internal state only when it is a stable, approved testability seam.'

eval_seed.good: Kills the boundary survivor and classifies the other two as unspecified or performance-only.
eval_seed.check: Runtime oracle: the candidate must kill the boundary mutant and must pass on both equivalent mutants.

finding: In agentic-mermaid, Stryker was the only dependency pulling in `minimatch`/`brace-expansion`; their advisories caused three dependency PRs and the 0.4.2 'security patch' version bump — a version never published, and the one the deploy gate has been skipping on.

suggested_edit.section: When it earns its cost: 'Estimate before running'
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Run the tool on demand (`npx`, `uvx`, `go run …@version`) rather than keeping a dependency nothing runs: its dependency tree still needs security patches.'

counterexample: An unpinned on-demand run (`npx tool` with no version) drifts between runs and breaks reproducibility, so the version must be pinned in the command. For a lane that runs on every PR, a locked dev dependency is easier to audit than ad-hoc downloads.

eval_seed.bad: Adds an override or bumps the package version and cuts a release.

Parity check now reports 100%'), atlas bfd1915 ('budget to match current build'), geist_fabrik 1acbc1e ('test count to 41'), agentic-mermaid 41a4468e ('re-pinned to live values'), and a private repo replaced parity oracles with 75 'frozen outcomes' captured from legacy code during its own test audit; output harvested from the code pinned a wrong ellipse label as correct.

suggested_edit.section: Write mode item 8 (Choose test values deliberately)
suggested_edit.text: Proposed: 'Every expected value comes from a spec or contract, a hand derivation, a reference implementation, a known-answer vector, or a property. A value obtained by running the code under test is a characterization: allowed only to protect a change to existing code, labelled, and retired afterwards; never the only oracle for new code.'

counterexample: Some outputs have no independent oracle short of reimplementation (exact layout coordinates, ML scores); there observed output plus review is the practical oracle, and labelling it a characterization should not mean deleting it. Output that is the shipped product (formatter output, published formats) is legitimately captured after review (CE-027). test-audit's junk pattern would reject these outright, which over-applies.

eval_seed.setup: A new `format_duration(seconds)` with a spec in its docstring ('90 → "1m 30s"', '3600 → "1h"'); the implementation has a bug: 3600 → '60m'. Prompt: 'Write tests for format_duration.'
eval_seed.bad: Runs the function and pastes `assert format_duration(3600) == '60m'`.
eval_seed.good: Derives expectations from the docstring spec; the 3600 case fails and exposes the bug.
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate tests against the buggy implementation (must fail) and the fixed one (must pass).

note: SKILL.md:174 forbids recomputing expectations with the SUT's logic but is silent on pasting the SUT's output, the 'equally dependent move' the research names.

finding: SKILL.md makes golden files the default oracle for complex output; in the hardest-hit repos 36.6% (agentic-mermaid, 301 of 823) and 43% (private repo A, 795 of 1,856) of non-merge commits touched a pinned artifact or source-text test, and sampled pin failures were mostly false alarms (10 of 14 in private repo A; 0 catches in 59 agentic-mermaid golden approvals). agentic-mermaid #357/#361 replaced 375 styled hashes with 16 readable SVG goldens and linkrank hashes with a property ('gap ≥ 223.5px').

testing_best_practices.passage: For transformations or complex generated output, use golden files with explicit review discipline; see `references/golden-file-testing.md`.

suggested_edit.section: SKILL.md Write mode (paragraph after the list); golden-file-testing.md intro
suggested_edit.text: Proposed oracle ladder, cheapest and most robust first: specified fields; parse then compare (DOM, AST, parsed YAML/JSON, rows from a real engine); property, metamorphic relation or differential; a tolerance justified by the spec; a small, normalised, reviewed golden; a hash only when the bytes are the product, with the artifact kept and a readable diff.

counterexample: For pipelines whose whole output is the contract (HTML→Markdown extraction, compilers, formatters), a reviewed golden of the full output is the most direct oracle, and the ladder's 'specified fields' rung would under-test them. Parse-then-compare can also hide differences that matter (attribute order inside a canonicalised XML signature).

eval_seed.bad: Byte-exact golden of the SVG string (fails on A).
eval_seed.good: Parses the SVG and asserts bar count, heights and labels (passes A, fails B).
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate tests against A (must pass) and B (must fail).

finding: The dominant agent pattern was a fix followed by a 'regression test' that greps for the fix's text: planet_cf b80a8d0 (+40 assertions for '20 mitigations'), atlas 560117f ('22 tests guarding the 5 audit fixes'), tasche f24cc91, geist_fabrik's release contracts and private repo A's `sourceBetween(...)` checks. They cannot fail on the pre-fix behaviour, break on any rename, and geist_fabrik's workflow-text tests pinned the text of the release bug they were meant to prevent.

testing_best_practices.passage: 1. **Red** — add a focused test that fails for the current bug/missing behavior.

test_audit.passage: Bug regression tests must fail on the pre-fix code for the intended reason and pass after the owner-boundary repair. A regression test that never demonstrably failed proves the mock, not the fix.

suggested_edit.section: SKILL.md red-green / Write mode; antipatterns.md detection table
suggested_edit.text: Proposed: 'A regression test must fail on the pre-fix behaviour. Grepping for the fix's text is not a regression test: it cannot fail on the old behaviour, and it breaks on renames. If behaviour cannot be reached, create a seam. Don't read source text.' Add a 'fix, then grep for the fix' detection row.

counterexample: Some fixes change text that is itself the contract (a user-facing error message, a security header value, a config key consumers read); asserting that text is behavioural. test-audit's retention bar keeps 'source inspection when it is the cheapest independent guard: it fails when the contract changes ... and survives an identifier-only refactor'.

eval_seed.setup: A fix adds `html.escape` to `render_comment()`. Prompt: 'Add a regression test for this fix.' Variants: the pre-fix build, and a behaviour-preserving refactor that moves escaping into a local `_esc` helper.

eval_seed.good: `assert '<script>' not in render_comment('<script>x</script>')`.
eval_seed.check: The candidate must fail on the pre-fix build and pass on the refactor. (A text-grep test also fails on the pre-fix build, so only the refactor variant separates the two.)

note: The existing red-green rule does not exclude text-grep tests, which are red before the fix because the fix's text is absent; the distinguishing check is survival of a behaviour-preserving rename (research §7 item 5).

finding: Source-text assertions were the dominant form outside the hash-heavy repos: private repo A peaked at 165 files and 4,054 `assert.match` calls (one file had 2,488 regexes), pythonbyexample has 180 of 962 assertions over CSS/JS/workflow text, and agentic-mermaid has 486 substring asserts on built HTML/CSS; in private repo A all 61 red unit CI runs that ran came from text, count or governance tests and none caught a product regression.

testing_best_practices.passage:
- **Source- or config-text assertions**: reading `src/`, CSS, docs, or workflow
  YAML and asserting substrings or regexes. They break on innocent edits and pass
  on real rendering or runtime bugs. Assert computed style, rendered output, or
  parsed-structure invariants ("every step after a precondition is gated on it"),

testing_best_practices.passage: 3. Record the actual outputs as assertions — even if they look wrong

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: scope characterization to changing existing code; label each test as a characterization; prefer relational or invariant characterisation (tuned ≤ baseline); after the change convert each pin to a specified assertion or delete it; never use it as the oracle for new code. test-types.md:211 ('Call the code and record actual outputs as assertions') gets the same retirement step.

counterexample: Feathers' characterization tests exist because no spec exists; converting pins to 'specified assertions' afterwards can be impossible for legacy behaviour nobody can specify, and deleting them removes the safety net for the next refactor. Retirement should be 'tighten or keep labelled', not mandatory deletion.

- Keep snapshots small and focused (one snapshot per behavior, not per test)
- Don't snapshot the entire program state — snapshot the part this test

counterexample: Normalising too aggressively hides real regressions (the same reference warns 'A digest that ignores fields gives false confidence'), and for whole-state save/load roundtrips breadth is the contract.

- The output is a tree, AST, rendered DOM, log sequence, or formatted text
- The same shape is asserted on across many tests (a single change should

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: drop 'more than ~5 fields' and 'cascade' as reasons to snapshot; first ask which fields the behaviour specifies, parse and compare those, and snapshot only a small, normalised projection.

layout change becomes a "rebind the hashes" commit, and a backend change needs a
second hash table. Prefer structural or perceptual goldens with a visible diff
(draw-command lists, text frames, SVG structure, images reviewed as images), and

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: allow hashes only for exactness the contract requires (release checksums, SRI, content addressing, crypto vectors), keep the artifact and print a readable diff on failure; hash inputs for provenance, not outputs as oracles.

counterexample: Where the bytes are the product (release tarball SHA, SRI, content-addressed stores, canonical sync-state hashes), hashes are the right oracle and structural checks would miss byte-level corruption (CE-027).

If you must keep hashes, re-pin
through a tool that records a written review of what changed.

counterexample: For legitimately pinned bytes (vendored model or font hashes, release checksums) a recorded review of each re-pin is cheap supply-chain hygiene; 'replace pins that churn' must not delete those.

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: 'Maintenance High unless normalised and small; bug power depends on review.'

counterexample: Small, normalised goldens on stable outputs (defuddle-style fixture tests) are genuinely low maintenance; a blanket 'High' could steer agents away from goldens where they are the cheapest oracle.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Choose a test strategy for a dashboard HTML renderer that changes weekly.' The harness then applies 5 weekly UI changes that do not alter specified behaviour.
eval_seed.bad: Whole-page goldens, citing low maintenance.
eval_seed.good: DOM assertions on specified elements, with at most small normalised snapshots.
eval_seed.check: Count the test edits each candidate needs across the 5 changes: good needs at most 1; bad needs at least 5.

finding: Incidental float values were pinned exactly: private repo A had 263 literals with 12+ decimals, including `0.2600000000000001`, and duplicated load coefficients; agentic-mermaid pinned A* heuristic values; and a real pacing fix was reverted because it moved a pinned fixture's RNG draws.

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: compare floats with a relative or ULP tolerance plus an absolute floor near zero; the tolerance is a spec decision — state it, justify it, and never loosen it to get to green.

counterexample: Where exact IEEE results are the contract (yaket's Python-port float parity, deterministic replay, decimal money arithmetic), a tolerance hides real divergence; differential-testing.md already warns 'Don't reach for a threshold when the output is actually exact.'

eval_seed.setup: `mean(xs)` implemented by naive summation. Prompt: 'Test this numeric routine.' Variants: (A) an implementation using `math.fsum` (differences ~1e-15); (B) an off-by-one denominator (`len(xs) - 1`).
eval_seed.good: `math.isclose(mean(xs), expected, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-12)` with spec-derived expected values.
eval_seed.check: The candidate must pass on A and fail on B.

note: differential-testing.md covers statistical thresholds for approximate outputs, not float comparison tolerances.

finding: Pixel-exact image baselines either never ran or were sealed to one machine: darwin-only screenshot baselines never ran in CI in 5 repos, and private repo A sealed per-DPR SHA-256s of renders 'recorded on the author's Chrome'; garten instead uses pixel probes plus Linux goldens in CI.

testing_best_practices.passage:
keep a loose tolerance and carry precision in structural assertions, or
  golden a deterministic intermediate.

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: use a perceptual threshold plus a pixel budget for images, stated and justified as a spec decision; never loosen it to get to green.

counterexample: For pixel-art or font-rendering engines where a single-pixel change is the bug, a perceptual threshold hides regressions; a tolerance chosen to make CI green is exactly what the rule warns against.

eval_seed.setup: A chart PNG test using exact pixel equality. Variants: (A) antialiasing differences from another renderer build (perceptually identical); (B) a legend colour swapped. Prompt: 'This visual test is flaky across machines; fix it.'
eval_seed.bad: Keeps exact equality (fails A) or sets a 10% pixel tolerance (passes B).
eval_seed.good: Uses a perceptual diff with a small, justified budget plus a structural assertion on legend colours (passes A, fails B).
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate against A (must pass) and B (must fail).

note: The current text says 'keep a loose tolerance' but asks for no perceptual metric or justification.

finding: The survey's control class (T6) is legitimate exactness: release tarball SHA and SRI, font and model file hashes, content-addressed stores, canonical sync-state hashes, crypto test vectors, ASCII terminal goldens that are the published output, yaket's Python-port float parity, and replay A == replay B; agentic-mermaid's rule after its clean-up is 'Hashes belong only on bytes we ship or fetch'.

test_audit.passage: Keep a test when it independently enforces a public API, plugin SDK, protocol, config, migration, storage, security, platform, default, prompt-byte, generated cross-language, package, release, or architecture contract.

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: list when exactness is legitimate — release checksums and SRI, crypto known-answer vectors, canonical encodings, content-addressed stores, published formats, formatter output, replay A == replay B, base vs head — so restraint probes keep it.

counterexample: 'Deterministic serialization is not canonical' (protobuf, IMPLEMENTATION_LOCK_IN:143): a list that includes 'formatter output' or 'published formats' can be stretched to any serializer a team happens to emit. The test is whether consumers depend on the exact bytes.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Our HMAC-SHA256 signer's tests compare byte-exact hex digests with RFC 4231 vectors; they're brittle, make them less brittle.' Planted bug: the key is padded one byte short.
eval_seed.bad: Replaces exact digests with length and hex-format checks.
eval_seed.good: Keeps the known-answer vectors byte-exact and explains why.
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate against the key-padding bug: good fails; bad passes.

note: differential-testing.md:136-138 already says exact outputs need equality, but only in the approximate-output section; nothing lists T6 cases for goldens and hashes. test-audit's retention bar keeps prompt-byte, package and release contracts.

finding: Fakes routed on SQL text instead of executing it: tasche has 405 `if "…" in sql` fake-routing lines and deleted its real-SQLite ranking tests in favour of `"MATCH" in sql`; planet_cf uses a regex MockD1. Restoring tasche's search tests on SQLite built from the migrations found a 500 on `?q=&sort=title_asc`, and porting flux-search's live-production tests offline through the real handler found FTS5 500s on hyphenated queries and bare AND/OR/NOT.

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: 'SQL-substring fakes are permissive environments. Load an in-memory engine from the migrations.'

counterexample: SQLite loaded from migrations is still not the production database: it reproduces D1's SQL but not its binding (`exec()` newline splitting, parameter caps; pilot CE-030), and Postgres-specific SQL will not run on SQLite at all; there a containerised real engine or recorded results are the honest rung.

eval_seed.setup: `search(q, sort)` builds SQL whose ORDER BY is ambiguous after a JOIN; tests use a fake that returns canned rows when `'MATCH' in sql`; migrations/ with an FTS5 table is available. Prompt: 'Add tests for sorting search results.'
eval_seed.bad: Adds more fake-routing cases for the sort parameter.
eval_seed.good: Runs the query on sqlite3 loaded from migrations.

finding: antipatterns.md #12 tells readers to 'Delete and re-record periodically' for both cassettes and snapshots, which institutionalises re-recording snapshots; Jest's own advice is to 'fix the bug before re-generating snapshots', and 8.2% of commits in snapshot-using projects update snapshots.

testing_best_practices.passage:
**Fix**: Delete and re-record periodically. Require explicit reviewer approval
for snapshot changes. Filter volatile data from cassettes.

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: 'Re-record cassettes; reduce and normalise snapshots rather than re-recording them.'

counterexample: Cassettes of external APIs genuinely go stale and must be re-recorded, so the split must keep that; and a snapshot whose contract legitimately changed must be regenerated. 'Reduce, don't re-record' applies to churn, not to intended changes.

eval_seed.setup: A snapshot suite where 12 snapshots fail after a refactor that only reordered JSON keys. Prompt: 'Fix the failing snapshot tests.'
eval_seed.bad: Runs the update flag and re-records all 12.
eval_seed.good: Sorts keys in the serializer so the snapshots pass unchanged.
eval_seed.check: After the fix, `git diff --stat __snapshots__` is empty for good; a planted value change still fails the good suite.

- test counts, lane counts, and timeouts quoted in docs match the runner's collection

suggested_edit.section: Pattern: Verification claims in project docs
suggested_edit.text: Proposed: don't quote volatile counts; generate them or omit them, and derive doc checks from the registry or CLI (olsen's docs-sync from the CLI's own help), not from copied literals.

counterexample: Exact counts are right where the count is the contract or a deliberate tripwire: keyboardia's lane contracts assert exact expected and skipped counts plus test identities so a dropped test cannot hide (praised at PORTFOLIO_VERIFICATION_AUDIT:359). The research's keyboardia step replaces them with 'no unexpected skips, no empty lane', which is weaker against silently dropped tests.

eval_seed.setup: README says 'We support 147 plugins'; a test asserts `len(PLUGINS) == 147`. Prompt: 'Add a new plugin.' A hidden follow-up adds a second plugin.
eval_seed.bad: Adds the plugin and bumps both numbers to 148.
eval_seed.good: Removes or generates the README count and replaces the test with registry-vs-docs set equality.
eval_seed.check: Apply the hidden second plugin (with its doc entry): the good suite passes with no further edits; the bad suite fails until 149 is typed in.

finding: SKILL.md's rule that every custom oracle needs a known-good and a known-bad input was read as 'prove the regex catches its own text', which produced dozens of source-text 'sabotage proofs'; private repo A's source-text tests needed tests of their own because 'state cannot be imported', and the audit found a private repo with 129 files of source-regex tests including 'mutants' that only test the regex.

testing_best_practices.passage: Every custom oracle, linter, validator, fixer, or eval grader needs a known-good input that passes and a known-bad input that fails

test_audit.passage: exact source, import, or string greps;

suggested_edit.text: Proposed: the oracle self-test rule applies to checkers of behaviour; a text-grep test is not an oracle to prove, it is a test to replace.

counterexample: Some text checkers are legitimate behaviour checkers of text artifacts (link checkers, prose linters, forbidden-API bans, secret scanners) and do need known-good and known-bad fixtures; the boundary is whether the text is the product or a proxy for code behaviour.

eval_seed.setup: A test `assert re.search(r'escape\(', src)` guards an XSS fix. Prompt: 'Prove this guard works (add a known-bad input).' Planted bug: escaping is applied to the wrong variable, so the text `escape(` is still present.
eval_seed.bad: Adds a 'sabotage proof' that deletes `escape(` from a copy of the source and asserts the regex fails.
eval_seed.good: Replaces the regex with a behavioural XSS test and shows it fails on an unescaped build.
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate against the wrong-variable bug: good fails; bad passes.

note: antipatterns #21 (shipped #28) already lists 'source-text "sabotage proofs" for regex change-detectors, which only test the regex', but only under mutation programs.

finding: agentic-mermaid's `nightly-route-mutation.yml` had 28 nightly/dispatch runs between 2026-06-19 and 2026-07-14 with zero successes: it was added inside an unrelated 33-file commit with no completed reference run, no notification and no owner, and its headline lane's measured work (~165 min) exceeded its 90-min timeout, so it failed on night one; scope grew from 4 to 14 lanes while red and a repair attempt reached 41 jobs before the surface was retired (agentic-mermaid #169).

testing_best_practices.passage: - Don't run on every commit — too slow. Run nightly or weekly.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'one complete retained baseline on the target CI; **no baseline, no schedule**; ... focused scope whose measured runtime fits its timeout and compute budget; a named owner and a result that either blocks a decision or notifies someone; ... an expiry/removal criterion and response to repeated operational failures.'

counterexample: Issue #20 itself asks for a keep-probe: a justified recurring lane (small module, measured 1-minute runtime, retained baseline, floor from measured history, named owner) must be accepted — 'the contract is a checklist, not a prohibition' (existing hidden eval E68). Applied as a ban, the contract blocks cheap, useful changed-code lanes.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Set up repository-wide nightly Stryker mutation testing with thresholds.break: 60 everywhere.' Fixture: the broad lane is estimated at 165 runner-minutes under a 90-minute timeout and has no completed CI baseline. (existing eval E64)
eval_seed.bad: Emits the cron workflow with `break: 60`.
eval_seed.good: Runs one manual baseline first, narrows to changed or critical modules that fit the timeout, keeps `break: null` until history exists, and names an owner and notify-or-block.
eval_seed.check: Parse the emitted workflow and config: no `schedule:` without a recorded baseline artifact; no `break` value; the selected scope's estimated runtime is below `timeout-minutes`.

note: The cadence line was the reference's only operational sentence (issue #20, Gap 1); verdict missing for the contract itself, and the cadence retraction is the next record.

testing_best_practices.passage: - Don't run on every commit — too slow. Run nightly or weekly.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Prefer changed-code, incremental, or review-time feedback' and test-types.md 'Mitigations: Prefer changed code or focused critical modules. Schedule only under the baseline/owner/budget/stop contract in `references/mutation-testing.md`.'

counterexample: Changed-code-only mutation never revisits old code whose tests were weakened by a test-only change; an occasional on-demand whole-module run (not a schedule) is still useful for a focused audit.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Add mutation testing to CI for our Python service; it is too slow for every commit.'
eval_seed.bad: Adds a nightly cron mutmut job over the repository.
eval_seed.good: Adds a pull-request job scoped to changed files (or a `workflow_dispatch` on-demand job) with a measured budget.

finding: The line '80% mutation score with 70% coverage > 95% coverage with 50% mutation score' was read as a ranking by score: one day after its first failed scheduled run agentic-mermaid wrote 'The mutation score is the truer number' into its testing strategy, then added fourteen uncalibrated `break: 60` floors, one of them above the lane's own recorded score. StrykerJS defaults to `break: null`, and Papadakis et al. found mutation-score/fault-detection correlations weak when controlling for suite size.

testing_best_practices.passage: - 80% mutation score with 70% coverage > 95% coverage with 50% mutation score.

suggested_edit.section: How to interpret a run; Operating a recurring lane
suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'A mutation score is not percent correctness, and `100%` is not a universal attainable target.' and 'Default to informational results. Prefer a changed-code policy such as "no newly surviving actionable mutant" over an absolute repository score. A requested round number is not calibration'.

counterexample: Higher scores among equal-sized suites can still guide improvement (the shipped text keeps this), and comparing like-for-like runs of the same lane is legitimate; 'not a target' must not become 'ignore the score'.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Our mutation score fell from 73% to 51% because the module tripled in size; write a plan to get it back above 70%.' (existing eval E65)
eval_seed.bad: Writes a plan whose acceptance criterion is a score of at least 70%.
eval_seed.good: Challenges the score framing, triages survivors (equivalent, unreachable, actionable) and notes that denominator growth is not a coverage regression.
eval_seed.check: Structured plan: its acceptance criteria contain no absolute score threshold, and it includes a survivor-classification step.

finding: The shipped skill never mentioned equivalent mutants (the caveat lived only in research/NOVEL_TESTING_TYPES.md, which does not ship) and defined a survivor as 'test gap found'; downstream, a lane that completed a real 1,889-mutant measurement scoring 30.17% was recorded as a CI failure. Schuler & Zeller found about 45% of undetected mutants equivalent at about 15 minutes each to classify, and keyboardia's 7/7 Stryker survivors were equivalent.

testing_best_practices.passage: 4. If all tests pass → mutant "survived" (test gap found)

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'First separate tool/run statuses ... Then classify actual survivors as: actionable behavior/oracle gap; equivalent or redundant mutation; dead/redundant code that should be removed; specified fault masking or graceful degradation; irrelevant/invalid operator for the domain', with the Schuler & Zeller caveat scoped to its sample.

counterexample: 'Equivalent' can become a convenient label for survivors nobody wants to kill; classification needs a stated reason per survivor (unobservable through the public interface, performance-only), and security-boundary survivors still need prompt triage.

eval_seed.setup: A mutation report for a parser with three survivors: `<` → `<=` on a length check where equal lengths are rejected earlier (equivalent); a removed logging call (arid); `return None` → `return []` on an error path (actionable). Prompt: 'Triage these survivors and add tests where needed.'
eval_seed.bad: Writes tests to kill all three, including asserting log calls.
eval_seed.good: Kills the error-path survivor and classifies the other two with reasons.
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate tests against the three mutants: they must kill the error-path mutant and must pass on the logging-removed and equivalent mutants.

finding: The skill text 'Surviving mutants in security code are P0 issues' was adopted downstream as 'a surviving mutant … is a P0' (aha), alongside 'no surviving mutants' as a definition of done in a repo with about 275 survivors in one package.

testing_best_practices.passage: - Surviving mutants in security code are P0 issues.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Triage security-boundary survivors promptly, but assign P0 only when a relevant, non-equivalent survivor plausibly represents a critical exploit or bypass.'

counterexample: In authorization or sanitizer code a survivor on the decision branch often is a real bypass; a lower default could leave one unfixed. The rule needs per-survivor triage, not a lower default priority.

eval_seed.setup: A mutation report for auth.py with two survivors: (a) `==` → `!=` on a role check that an identical earlier check already guards (equivalent); (b) `>=` → `>` on token expiry (a token stays valid one second too long). Prompt: 'Prioritise these survivors.'
eval_seed.bad: Marks both P0.
eval_seed.good: Marks (b) high with a test that kills it and classifies (a) as equivalent with a reason.
eval_seed.check: Run the candidate tests: they kill (b) and pass on (a); the structured priorities differ.

note: Issue #20 does not mention P0 classification; the evidence is the 2026-09 audit's mutation-cost attribution, and the retraction shipped in #27 with #20's edits (CHANGELOG.md:21). Filed under source #20 per this file's mapping.

finding: agentic-mermaid enrolled every module family in its mutation lane through a CI-enforced test, against the skill's 'Focus on critical modules, not the whole codebase'; its family-citizenship work made the mutation lane a universal registration surface (#48, #49). Issue #20 proposed an eval for this universal-enrollment trap.

testing_best_practices.passage: - Focus on critical modules, not the whole codebase.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Do not enroll every module merely for parity. Start with changed, covered code or a small critical module.' (antipatterns #21 later added the signal 'tests that enforce enrollment in the mutation lane'.)

counterexample: Registry-driven enrollment is exactly what combinatorial-testing.md recommends for conformance cases (CE-014); an agent could over-apply 'no universal enrollment' to conformance matrices, where every registry member must be covered.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Add a mutation lane config for every module in src/ so coverage is consistent.' src/ has 40 modules; two handle auth and money.
eval_seed.bad: Generates 40 configurations.
eval_seed.good: Configures on-demand runs for the 2 high-consequence modules and explains why the rest are not enrolled.
eval_seed.check: Count the mutation targets in the emitted configuration: good names at most the 2–3 critical modules; bad names 40.

finding: The research note claimed 'NIST research shows 2-way testing catches 60-90% of bugs; 3-way catches 90-99%', and #21 asked for primary-source qualification. The primary sources describe the interaction degree of historical failures (e.g. NIST SP 800-142's NASA example: cumulative 67% one-way, 93% two-way, 98% three-way), not a guaranteed detection rate, and say pairwise may miss 10–40% or more.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Historical studies found many observed failures involved few factors, but the distributions varied by system. This motivates low-order interaction coverage; it does not mean pairwise or 3-way testing catches a universal percentage of bugs.'

counterexample: Stripping all numbers can make agents under-use pairwise where it is clearly cost-effective; scoped historical figures remain useful as motivation when labelled as observations from specific systems.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Write the release-note paragraph justifying replacing our 4,500-case Cartesian matrix with pairwise.' Answer format: JSON with fields {justification, claimed_detection_rate, evidence}.
eval_seed.bad: Claims pairwise catches 60–90% (or 90%+) of bugs.
eval_seed.good: States that pairwise guarantees coverage of modelled 2-way tuples, cites local fault history or shadow evidence, and keeps known high-order regressions.
eval_seed.check: Parse the JSON: claimed_detection_rate must be null and evidence must reference shadow or fault-replay results.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Known regressions are mandatory even when their 4-way or higher interaction is absent from the generated array.'

counterexample: Fixed regressions accumulate; one whose code path was deleted, or whose interaction is now impossible under the constraints, should be retired rather than kept forever because it is 'mandatory'.

eval_seed.good: Keeps it as a mandatory fixed test beside the pairwise rows and explains why.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: an exact-set test (`expected = set(canonical_registry)` ... `assert modeled == expected`), then 'inject a fake registry member in an isolated registry, prove it is enrolled automatically, give it deliberately broken behavior, and prove the generated contract fails for the intended oracle.'

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Integrate constraints during generation or feasibility solving. Generating an unconstrained array and deleting invalid rows can silently remove the only row covering a required feasible tuple.' and 'Choose elevated groups from architecture, hazard analysis, changed coupling, or repaired-fault history'.

counterexample: For spaces small enough to exhaust cheaply, covering-array machinery adds modelling cost and a generator dependency for no gain; and issue #22 shows some cross-products need not be exercised at all because an upstream layer decides the property.

eval_seed.setup: Prompt: 'Design a ten-minute blocking portfolio for 15 renderer families, 16 Looks, 21 Palettes, 4 outputs, 5 boundaries and 4 runtimes; some combinations are invalid.' Answer must include the generated rows as CSV and the constraints. (existing eval E66)

finding: #21 asked for multi-objective selection across runtime and environment startup, flake and rerun cost, maintenance and baseline review, triage, and bug-finding power; in agentic-mermaid two central Style evidence files alone made more than 1,100 render/output calls and the visible Style/Palette gates took about 37 s serially.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Keep hard obligations first, then compare feasible portfolios across a cost vector ... Do not collapse unlike quantities into one magic score unless the project has approved and sensitivity-tested the weights. Prefer a Pareto view'.

counterexample: For a small suite a single rough metric (CI minutes) is often enough; a full Pareto analysis is overhead that #21's scale justifies but a 50-test suite does not.

eval_seed.setup: Three candidate portfolios with vectors (CPU minutes, flake %, maintenance edits per month, sabotage kills): P1 (10, 2, 4, 9), P2 (12, 3, 5, 8), P3 (6, 1, 6, 7). Prompt: 'Pick the best portfolio.'
eval_seed.bad: Combines the columns into one weighted score with invented weights.
eval_seed.good: Drops the dominated P2 and presents the P1/P3 trade-off for the owner to decide.
eval_seed.check: Structured output: P2 is excluded as dominated and no composite score is reported.

finding: #21 asked how to calibrate costs from CI history (per-test and per-job durations, retry and flake history, failure attribution, mutation/sabotage kills, changed-file data) 'without turning noisy wall-clock measurements into flaky gates'.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: a three-row table (stable policy / versioned calibration / raw telemetry: 'Diagnosis only; never directly changes gates') and 'retain timeout observations as censored failures ... Sparse or unobserved history is "unknown," not measured zero.'

counterexample: Some telemetry should change gates quickly: a test that starts timing out on every run is a real regression, so 'never directly changes gates' must not delay quarantining a broken lane.

eval_seed.setup: CI history JSON for 20 tests over 30 runs; one test has only 3 runs and another has timeouts at the 60 s cap. Prompt: 'Compute p90 durations to rebalance the shards.'
eval_seed.bad: Treats the 3-run test as measured and the timed-out runs as completing at 60 s.
eval_seed.good: Marks the sparse test unknown, treats timeouts as censored (at least 60 s), and reports sample counts.
eval_seed.check: Structured output: the sparse test's p90 is null/unknown; the timed-out test's p90 is flagged as a lower bound of at least 60 s.

finding: #21's acceptance criteria require validating a replacement portfolio with historical fault injection, mutation/sabotage or shadow runs before deleting existing tests; agentic-mermaid's 4,500-render replacement used shadow evidence and measured p90 cost (#193).

test_audit.passage: Before claiming completion, have independent reviewers compare deleted coverage against the keepers, one reviewer per boundary group. They look for contracts that lost their only proof.

suggested_edit.text: Shipped: 'Run old and proposed portfolios in shadow before deleting tests: mechanically verify all one-way and interaction obligations; replay repaired faults and retain every discriminating regression; run representative mutation/sabotage probes ...; keep a rotating randomized full-suite/holdout sample'.
